sector: Healthcare Services (NZ Primary Care / Aged Residential Care Medical Services)
overview: Third Age Health Services Limited is New Zealand's leading dedicated provider of managed primary medical services to the aged residential care (ARC) sector, delivering GP and Nurse Practitioner-led care to residents in rest homes, private hospitals, secure dementia units and retirement villages nationwide, alongside a smaller general practice business serving the wider community in Auckland and Hawke's Bay. Now 15 years old, TAH operates as a national platform built through organic facility wins and disciplined bolt-on acquisitions of founder-owned ARC medical practices. Revenue is funded predominantly through NZ Government primary care capitation (via PHOs) and fee-for-service consultations, and the company operates exclusively within New Zealand.

business_model.summary: TAH generates revenue through two segments: ARC Medical Services (FY26 revenue $14.921M, +27% YoY, ~66% of total) and Community General Practice ($7.567M, +3.2% YoY, ~34% of total). Revenue is largely recurring — monthly capitation payments from PHOs based on enrolled-patient counts and demographics, supplemented by per-visit consultation fees. The model is asset-light (clinicians deliver care within client-owned ARC facilities or leased GP clinic premises under service contracts), giving high operating leverage as the patient base scales. TAH grows the ARC segment through bolt-on acquisition of small, founder-owned ARC medical practices at modest multiples, integrated using its 'Third Age Way of Working' (TAWoW) Kaizen-based operating system, and has explicitly stopped acquiring further Community GP practices after negative experience with small-practice economics (e.g. Belmont Medical Centre closure, FY26).

revenue_streams.name: Community General Practice (capitation + consultation)
revenue_streams.trend: stable/low-growth, patient attrition offset by pricing

business_model.customer_type: B2B (ARC facility operators as primary clients; NZ Government / Health NZ / PHOs as primary funder; individual ARC residents and GP patients as end-users)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. National ARC footprint including Auckland, Wellington/Lower North Island, Northland, Canterbury (via ARC Health, Sept 2025) and Bay of Plenty (via Cicada Health, Sept 2025); Community GP concentrated in Auckland (Devonport, Ponsonby) and Hawke's Bay. No foreign operations or currency exposure.

main_competitors: Independent/owner-operator GPs and small regional GP networks servicing ARC facilities on an ad hoc basis
Large integrated aged-care operators (Ryman Healthcare, Bupa NZ, Summerset, Oceania Healthcare, Metlifecare, Arvida) — indirect competition where facilities manage medical services in-house
Locum GP/NP staffing agencies (compete for scarce clinician supply rather than for facility contracts)
General practice owner-operators and PHOs more broadly, for Community GP patient enrolments
competitive_position.market_position: Largest dedicated national provider of managed primary medical care to ARC facilities in New Zealand, with an estimated ~17-18% share of the ARC medical services market and a stated medium-term target of 20%. No competitor operates at equivalent national scale in this specific niche. Recently named sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand (Sept 2025).

moat_factors.description: National footprint across ARC facilities, expanded into Canterbury and Bay of Plenty via the FY26 ARC Health and Cicada Health acquisitions, gives TAH a clinician network, rostering infrastructure, and management system that small-scale competitors cannot easily replicate. Facility relationships tend to be sticky given the operational burden of switching medical service providers.

Digital Clinical Portal live in 30+ facilities (from 13 at March 2025), supporting 900+ scheduled clinical rounds; Phase 2/3 development underway. Paired with TAH's independently-audited 'Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard' (Elder Care Standards), this creates differentiation versus the fragmented visiting-clinician norm and could become a de facto sector benchmark.

moat_factors.factor: PHO contract relationships and regulatory/administrative complexity
moat_factors.description: Capitation revenue flows via PHO agreements recognised as intangible assets on acquisition. Navigating ARC-specific enrolment rules and maintaining PHO relationships is a meaningful barrier for new entrants. Sole preferred partner status with the Aged Care Association New Zealand reinforces sector standing and provides a platform for sector-level advocacy.

NP Development Programme (first graduates in the pipeline) and structured GP training pathways provide a partially self-sustaining talent funnel in an otherwise severely undersupplied labour market — a structural differentiator smaller operators cannot fund.

The 'Third Age Way of Working' provides a standardised, low-cost playbook for onboarding new facilities and integrating acquisitions, difficult for competitors to replicate quickly and supportive of margin durability even through a period of deliberate margin compression to protect service quality (FY26).

weaknesses: Small absolute scale (~NZ$22.5M FY26 revenue, ~NZ$44-49M market cap through 2026) limits negotiating leverage with Health NZ/PHOs and constrains access to low-cost capital
Community GP segment (~34% of revenue) continues to lose enrolled patients (-4.8% YoY in FY26, third consecutive year of decline) despite improved profitability from cost discipline
Dependent on an acutely thin clinician labour market — management states ARC growth is 'constrained' by clinical workforce availability, not by demand

FY26 letter to shareholders disclosed the forced closure of the small Belmont Medical Centre practice after safety incidents with disruptive patients, illustrating operational fragility of small acquired practices and informing management's decision to stop acquiring further Community GP practices
Minority-owned subsidiaries (Hub Aged Care 70%, ARC Health 80%, Cicada Health 70%, and other GP entities) create governance complexity and NCI dilution of parent earnings

NZX micro-cap illiquidity; share price swung between roughly NZ$2.50 and NZ$7.50 over FY26 (a ~3x range), which the Chairman explicitly stated does not reflect a realistic assessment of intrinsic value in either direction

Key leadership transition risk: Niomi Fleming, ARC business General Manager, announced she will step down for health reasons at end of July 2026, shortly after being confirmed in the permanent GM role

growth_drivers: NZ demographic tailwind: population aged 65+ was ~16.6% of NZ in 2023 (up from 12.3% in 2006) and is projected to reach ~28% by 2073; the 65+ dependency ratio is projected to rise from ~25 per 100 working-age people (2024) to 43-57 per 100 by 2078. This is a multi-decade, non-cyclical structural demand driver for ARC medical services.

ARC market share expansion: TAH targets ~20% of the ARC medical services market (from an estimated ~17-18% currently), via a mix of organic facility wins (management notes ongoing inbound interest from ARC facilities, constrained mainly by clinical workforce availability) and further bolt-on acquisitions.

Bolt-on acquisitions at attractive multiples, ARC-focused: Hub Aged Care (April 2024, $742k, Wellington), ARC Health (Sept 2025, $1.10M, Canterbury), Cicada Health (Sept 2025, $0.86M, Bay of Plenty) — all immediately EBITDA-accretive with founders remaining as active co-owners. Chairman has explicitly stated the company will not allocate further capital to acquiring additional Community GP practices, sharpening capital allocation toward ARC and adjacent opportunities. In FY26 management also evaluated (but did not complete) acquisitions outside healthcare in life-safety, compliance, and maintenance/repair/operations sectors, reflecting a broadened but disciplined capital allocation lens.

ARC capitation rate increases and reweighting: the largest PHO capitation uplift in over a decade (9.69% total government uplift) took effect from July 2025. A new capitation formula effective 1 July 2026 will incorporate age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality and socioeconomic deprivation — expected to better reflect TAH's older, higher-acuity ARC patient population and could be a structural positive for capitation revenue per patient.

Digital Clinical Portal rollout: live in 30+ facilities as of H1 FY26 (from 13 at March 2025), supporting 900+ scheduled clinical rounds; Phase 2 in development, Phase 3 in planning. Reduces per-patient administrative cost, improves care quality metrics, and strengthens client retention.

AI and virtual care: AI transcription tools reducing clinician documentation burden; telehealth/virtual care solutions extending after-hours ARC coverage, effectively expanding clinician capacity without proportional headcount growth.

Elder Care Standards adoption: TAH's independently-assessed Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard, if adopted more broadly across the sector or referenced in future regulation, would give TAH first-mover compliance advantage and enhanced client stickiness.

business.description: The large majority of TAH's revenue ultimately flows from Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora), either as capitation via PHOs or consultation fee schedules. Any reduction in ARC-specific or GP capitation rates, tightening of enrolment criteria, or continued Health NZ fiscal constraint (Health NZ was placed under Commissioner control in 2024 amid a structural deficit) would directly compress revenue and margins. TAH is a price-taker in the government-funded primary care system with limited negotiating leverage.

business.risk: Clinical workforce shortage and wage inflation
business.description: NZ faces a structural GP/NP shortage (over half of GPs aged 50+, a meaningful share of practices closed to new enrolments, a multi-year projected GP deficit). ARC growth is explicitly capacity-constrained by clinician availability per the FY26 letter to shareholders ('our primary operational risk remains the supply of clinical talent... failing to fill vacancies would directly lead to a loss of business'). Cost of services (predominantly clinician remuneration) rose to $11.4M in FY26 (~51% of revenue) from $9.18M (~48%) in FY25, and FY26 margin compression in the ARC segment was a deliberate trade-off to secure clinical coverage.

business.risk: Community GP segment structural decline and small-practice fragility
business.description: Community GP enrolled patients fell for a third consecutive year, down 4.8% to 19,383 in FY26, driven by doctor departures and unfilled vacancies (now filled). The FY26 letter disclosed TAH was forced to close its small Belmont Medical Centre site after safety incidents with disruptive patients — a 'clear reminder of the operational fragility of acquiring very small practices' — and management has explicitly ruled out further Community GP acquisitions. EastMed remains the segment's most financially marginal CGU with limited goodwill headroom.

Niomi Fleming, only recently confirmed as permanent General Manager of the ARC business (TAH's strongest-performing segment), announced she will step down for health reasons at the end of July 2026. Executive Chairman John Fernandes (a hands-on capital allocator) and Founder/Director Bevan Walsh remain central to strategy and culture; the company's small management team increases disruption risk from any senior departure. Lucy Wu was appointed Acting GM of Community GP to lead its turnaround.

TAH completed four ARC acquisitions in roughly two years, each with founders retained as minority co-owners (70-80% TAH ownership). Rapid growth in subsidiary count adds integration complexity, and alignment with active founder-operators on strategy, compensation or eventual exit terms could create friction. Deferred contingent consideration on ARC Health ($280k) and Cicada Health ($219k) is payable September 2026 if performance conditions are met.

TAH issued a patient communications update in January 2026 relating to the MMH cybersecurity breach in late 2025 (MMH is a third-party patient portal used across NZ primary care). TAH patient data may have been compromised; no material financial impact has been disclosed, but reputational risk exists.

financial.risk: Small-cap illiquidity and volatile market pricing
financial.description: With roughly 9.95-10.9 million shares and a market cap in the NZ$44-50M range through 2026, TAH is a micro-cap with thin trading volumes. The Chairman disclosed the share price swung between roughly NZ$2.50 and NZ$7.50 during FY26 — a ~3x range he described as an unrealistic assessment of intrinsic value at both ends. This limits institutional participation, widens bid-ask spreads, and constrains TAH's ability to use equity as acquisition currency.

financial.risk: Bank debt and lease liabilities at floating/contracted rates
financial.description: As at March 2026, TAH carried $1.09M in bank loans (current + non-current) and $2.26M in lease liabilities, funded partly via a line of credit (drawn briefly for the ARC Health/Cicada Health acquisitions and promptly repaid). Total debt remains modest relative to FY26 EBITDA of $5.75M. Interest rate risk is limited but real; declining NZ OCR (from 2023-24 peak) is a modest tailwind for borrowing costs.

financial.risk: Intangible asset concentration and amortisation growth
financial.description: Intangible assets grew to $6.67M at March 2026 (from $4.77M at March 2025) as ARC Health and Cicada Health goodwill/PHO-agreement intangibles were recognised. Amortisation and depreciation rose to $1.07M in FY26 (from $841k in FY25), structurally reducing statutory NPAT relative to underlying NPATA as the acquisition portfolio grows. EastMed and other marginal CGUs carry limited goodwill headroom.

regulatory.risk: Health NZ funding reform and capitation reweighting
regulatory.description: The capitation funding formula (unchanged since 2002) is being revised, with the new formula (incorporating age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality, and socioeconomic deprivation) effective from 1 July 2026. For TAH's largely elderly, high-acuity patient base this is expected to be a net positive, but transition arrangements and the precise revenue impact remain uncertain until implemented and observed in FY27 results.

A government-convened advisory process on aged-care funding models has been underway, with potential implementation from 2027. Any shift toward bundled ARC-operator payments rather than direct GP capitation could fundamentally alter TAH's revenue model, though the stated government policy intent (reducing hospital pressure via stronger community/ARC care) is broadly supportive of TAH's role.

Ongoing Health NZ structural reform has reduced the number of PHOs nationally. If TAH's PHO partners merge or consolidate, contract renegotiation could affect capitation rates or enrolment terms. No specific adverse developments were identified in the review period.

macro.description: Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora remains under fiscal pressure following Commissioner control imposed in 2024. While the FY26 capitation uplift (9.69%) was the largest in a decade, TAH's revenue per enrolled patient remains entirely dependent on future government funding decisions; any capitation freeze or reduction would directly compress margins given TAH's limited pricing power.

macro.risk: NZ economic conditions affecting GP co-payments
macro.description: TAH's ARC business is largely insulated from the economic cycle (ARC residents are government-funded). The Community GP segment earns some fee-for-service co-payments that could soften in a downturn, but this is a modest share of total revenue.

execution.description: Enrolled GP patients have declined for three straight years despite leadership changes (Lucy Wu appointed Acting GM) and process improvements that lifted segment profitability. Management states 'we are not satisfied with a shrinking patient roster' and 'a meaningful amount of work remains.' Continued decline increases the risk of further site closures (as with Belmont) and goodwill impairment at marginal CGUs like EastMed.

In FY26 management evaluated (via term sheets that ultimately did not proceed) acquisitions outside healthcare in life-safety, compliance, and maintenance/repair/operations sectors. While no deal was completed, continued pursuit of adjacent-sector M&A introduces execution risk if management ventures into unfamiliar industries, even though discipline shown to date (walking away from term sheets that didn't meet return criteria) is a positive signal.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ aged-care demand is structurally growing on demographics: the 65+ share of population rose from 12.3% (2006) to 16.6% (2023) and is projected to reach ~28% by 2073, with the 65+ dependency ratio roughly doubling by 2078. ARC facility supply is constrained by land, construction costs and staffing, keeping occupancy high and demand for in-facility medical services growing in parallel. The primary care sector faces chronic structural underfunding (capitation formula unchanged since 2002) but received its largest uplift in a decade for FY26, with a demographically-reweighted formula from July 2026. GP/NP supply is structurally short and unlikely to improve materially for 5-10 years.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Very low. ARC medical services are non-discretionary healthcare funded primarily by government capitation; Community GP services are partially fee-based (co-payments) but still predominantly government-funded. TAH's revenue has grown through COVID-19 and NZ's 2023-24 economic slowdown without interruption.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity — total debt (bank loans + leases) of roughly $3.3M at March 2026 relative to FY26 EBITDA of $5.75M. Indirect benefit from a declining NZ OCR (down from a 5.5% 2023-24 peak) reduces borrowing costs and supports continued acquisition financing.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None. TAH operates exclusively in New Zealand; revenue, costs and capital structure are entirely NZD-denominated.
key_input_costs: GP and Nurse Practitioner remuneration (largest cost; cost of services rose to ~51% of revenue in FY26 from ~48% in FY25, reflecting deliberate investment in clinical coverage)
Technology and digital enablement (Digital Clinical Portal build-out)
Lease costs for GP clinic premises

recent_developments.event: TAH released its Q1 FY27 trading update (revised from a planned 24 July 2026 date) and declared a Q1 FY27 interim dividend, consistent with the fixed quarterly dividend policy adopted from FY26. Detailed figures were not yet reflected in available secondary sources as of this analysis; investors should refer directly to the NZX announcement for Q1 FY27 NPAT and segment KPIs.

TAH released its audited FY26 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2026): revenue $22.488M (+17.9% YoY), EBITDA $5.747M, underlying EBIT $5.291M (margin 23.5%, +1.1pp YoY), statutory NPAT $3.091M (+24.7%), underlying NPATA $3.634M (+25.9%), diluted EPS 28.38 cents (+24.8%), ROE 55.9% (TTM), ROCE 44.1% (TTM). ARC segment revenue grew 27% to $14.921M with 7,138 enrolled patients; Community GP revenue grew 3.2% to $7.567M but enrolled patients fell 4.8% to 19,383. Full-year dividend 16.00 cps (+8.8% YoY). The Chairman's letter disclosed the forced closure of the Belmont Medical Centre practice after safety incidents, confirmed the company will not acquire further Community GP practices, and disclosed that ARC business GM Niomi Fleming will step down for health reasons at end of July 2026. Management evaluated but did not complete several non-healthcare acquisition opportunities (life-safety, compliance, MRO sectors) during the year.

TAH released preliminary unaudited FY26 full-year results broadly consistent with the subsequent audited figures, describing the FY27 operating backdrop as 'difficult' given ongoing workforce shortages and cost pressures.

TAH reported Q3 FY26 performance: quarterly NPAT of $818k, up 16.7% YoY. Board declared a Q3 FY26 interim dividend of 4.00 cents per share (fully imputed), consistent with the fixed quarterly dividend policy.

TAH issued a patient information update regarding the Manage My Health (MMH) cybersecurity breach that occurred in late 2025; MMH is a third-party patient portal used across NZ primary care. No material financial impact was disclosed.

TAH released H1 FY26 results (six months to 30 September 2025): revenue $10.653M (+13.2% YoY), NPAT $1.520M (+31.7% YoY), underlying NPATA $1.742M (+28.0% YoY). ARC enrolled patients 7,159 (including 1,684 from the ARC Health and Cicada Health acquisitions); organic ARC enrolled patients grew 3.7% YoY. GP enrolled patients 20,032 (-2.4% YoY). Digital Clinical Portal live in 30+ facilities, supporting 900+ scheduled clinical rounds. Niomi Fleming and Lucy Wu appointed Acting GMs of the newly separated ARC and Community GP business units respectively.

TAH acquired 80% of ARC Health Limited (Canterbury, $1.10M total consideration) and 70% of Cicada Health Limited (Bay of Plenty/Tauranga, $0.86M total consideration), effective 1 September 2025, funded from cash and a brief line-of-credit drawdown (promptly repaid). Both were immediately EBITDA-accretive with founders remaining active co-owners. Deferred contingent consideration of $280k (ARC Health) and $219k (Cicada Health) payable September 2026 subject to performance conditions.

TAH announced its 'Residential Care Medical Service Provider Standard' (Elder Care Standards), independently assessed by a Ministry of Health-designated auditing agency, and was appointed sole preferred medical services partner by the Aged Care Association New Zealand.

NZ Minister of Health announced a revised primary care capitation funding formula (incorporating age, sex, multimorbidity, rurality and socioeconomic deprivation), effective 1 July 2026 — potentially favourable for TAH's older, higher-acuity ARC patient population.

Health New Zealand and sector representatives agreed the largest capitation funding uplift in over a decade: 9.69% total government uplift for FY26 (6.43% capitation uplift plus 50% of $30M contingent funding), effective from approximately July 2025.

TAH released its FY25 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2025): revenue $19.081M (+26%), NPAT $2.478M (+79%), underlying NPATA $2.886M (+69%), underlying EBIT margin 22.4% (vs 17.2% prior year). ARC facilities grew from 67 to 90 (+34%). Board adopted a fixed quarterly dividend of 4.00 cps from FY26 (replacing the prior ~75%-of-NPAT payout ratio policy).

guidance.as_of: FY26 Annual Report (26 June 2026) and Q1 FY27 Trading Update (31 July 2026)

items.notes: FY26 letter to shareholders: 'We expect the operating environment to remain difficult. Workforce shortages and cost pressures are a fact of life, and we are not expecting any near-term relief.' Priority for FY27 is to build on FY26 progress via TAWoW operational discipline while remaining frugal; no explicit numerical FY27 revenue or earnings target has been disclosed.

items.vs_prior: maintained at the fixed quarterly rate established for FY26
items.notes: Policy changed from a ~75%-of-NPAT payout ratio to a fixed quarterly cents-per-share amount from FY26, providing shareholders greater certainty while preserving flexibility to reinvest for growth. FY26 total dividend of 16.00 cps was up 8.8% on FY25's 14.71 cps.

items.target: ~20% of the NZ ARC population medium-term (originally framed as a 5-year target from FY24)
items.notes: Estimated at ~17-18% as of FY25/FY26. Organic growth is constrained by clinical workforce availability rather than by facility demand; the new capitation formula from July 2026 may lift funding per patient for TAH's higher-acuity population.

items.target: Continued bolt-on ARC acquisitions; explicit halt on further Community GP acquisitions; opportunistic evaluation of non-healthcare recurring-revenue businesses
items.vs_prior: refined vs prior year — explicitly narrower on Community GP (no further acquisitions), explicitly broader outside healthcare
items.notes: Chairman's FY26 letter: searching for 'mission critical services or products, with recurring and predictable revenue, a demonstrated ability to generate free cash flow and earn returns on tangible capital in line with our expectations,' from founders 'planning for their own third age.' Deferred contingent consideration for ARC Health ($280k) and Cicada Health ($219k) due September 2026 if performance conditions are met.

guidance.management_commentary: FY26 Chairman's letter (John Fernandes, Executive Chairman): 'While the underlying demand for aged residential care and primary care continues to grow... the broader system is struggling to keep up... Our primary operational risk remains the supply of clinical talent... We expect the operating environment to remain difficult. Workforce shortages and cost pressures are a fact of life, and we are not expecting any near-term relief.' On valuation and capital allocation: 'Neither of these prices [NZ$2.50-$7.50 range during FY26] was a realistic assessment of per-share intrinsic value... our focus will always be on maximising the average annual rate of increase in intrinsic value per share.'

bull_case: Structural demographic tailwind is among the most powerful and certain long-duration growth drivers available on the NZX: NZ's 65+ population share is projected to nearly double by 2073, and the 85+ cohort (highest ARC utilisation) grows fastest of all. TAH is the only NZX-listed pure-play services provider (not a property owner like Ryman or Summerset) positioned to capture this trend directly.

Consolidation of a fragmented niche at attractive valuations, using a proven, repeatable playbook: Hub Aged Care, ARC Health and Cicada Health were each acquired at modest total consideration relative to the EBITDA/revenue contributed, immediately accretive, with founders retained as engaged co-owners. Management has shown capital discipline by walking away from non-healthcare term sheets that didn't meet return criteria.

The FY26 capitation uplift (largest in a decade) and the demographically-reweighted formula effective July 2026 should lift capitation revenue per enrolled patient for TAH's specific patient mix (elderly, high-acuity) without requiring volume growth — a funding tailwind largely outside TAH's control but directly beneficial to its economics.

High and resilient profitability with real operating leverage: FY26 underlying EBIT margin 23.5% (up from 22.4% in FY25), ROCE 44.1% and ROE 55.9% (TTM), despite deliberate margin compression in the ARC segment to secure clinical coverage. The business is asset-light, capital-light, and converts a high proportion of EBIT to free cash flow, supporting a fixed and growing quarterly dividend (16 cps annualised, +8.8% YoY).

Sole preferred medical services partner status with the Aged Care Association New Zealand and the independently-audited Elder Care Standards give TAH a sector-endorsed platform that could accelerate facility wins and, if adopted more broadly, create additional switching costs and regulatory-style moat.
bear_case: Growth is decelerating and management has explicitly and repeatedly guided to a 'difficult' operating environment for FY27, in contrast to the exceptional FY20-25 growth run. Community GP enrolled patients have now declined for three consecutive years, culminating in the forced closure of the Belmont practice after safety incidents — a tangible example of execution risk in the segment the Chairman has now stepped back from expanding.

Health NZ fiscal pressure is the single largest systemic risk: Health NZ remains under Commissioner control following a 2024 structural deficit, and TAH's revenue is almost entirely dependent on government funding decisions it cannot control. A future capitation freeze, reduction, or restructuring of ARC funding (e.g. shifting to bundled facility-operator payments) could materially compress the revenue model with little notice.

The clinical workforce shortage is structural and, by management's own account, is the binding constraint on ARC growth — not demand. Cost of services rose to ~51% of revenue in FY26 (from ~48% in FY25) as TAH paid up to secure clinical coverage, and no near-term relief is expected; this could keep compressing margins even as revenue grows.

Micro-cap illiquidity and extreme price volatility (the Chairman noted a ~3x trading range, NZ$2.50-$7.50, during FY26 alone, calling neither level a fair reflection of intrinsic value) make TAH difficult to size meaningfully in a portfolio, and the company lacks efficient access to equity capital markets to fund larger-scale M&A.

Leadership transition risk has crystallised: Niomi Fleming, only recently confirmed as permanent GM of the strongest-performing ARC segment, is stepping down for health reasons at the end of July 2026, adding near-term execution uncertainty just as the Community GP turnaround (under Acting GM Lucy Wu) also remains unresolved after three years of patient attrition.
